questions.stem: The Taj Mahal at Agra was built by which Mughal emperor in memory of his wife?
questions.explanation: The Taj Mahal — built 1632-53 by Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Arjumand Banu Begum (titled Mumtaz Mahal), who died in 1631 giving birth to their 14th child. Chief architect Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983). Other Shah Jahan monuments — Red Fort and Jama Masjid (Delhi), Moti Masjid (Agra). Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri; Jahangir's major work was the Shalimar Bagh (Kashmir); Aurangzeb built the Bibi ka Maqbara in Aurangabad.

questions.stem: Akbar's new religion, which combined Hindu, Muslim, Zoroastrian and Christian elements, was called:
questions.explanation: Din-i-Ilahi ('Divine Faith') — Akbar proclaimed it in 1582 as a syncretic belief system, though it gained few converts beyond his court. 'Sulh-i-Kul' ('peace with all') was Akbar's broader policy of religious tolerance — not the religion itself. Sufism is Islamic mysticism; Bhakti was a parallel devotional movement within Hinduism. The Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri was the interfaith discussion hall that inspired Din-i-Ilahi.

questions.stem: The 'Mansabdari' system of ranking nobles in the Mughal administration was introduced by:
questions.explanation: Akbar introduced Mansabdari around 1575 to unify military command, civil administration and revenue. Each 'mansabdar' had two numerical ranks — 'zat' (personal status, salary) and 'sawar' (number of cavalry he had to maintain). The highest rank under Akbar was 7,000. The system gradually decayed in quality under Akbar's successors, contributing to 18th-century decline.

questions.stem: The famous Mughal capital city Fatehpur Sikri was built by:
questions.explanation: Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri (1571-85) as his capital, 40 km from Agra, to honour the Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti who had foretold the birth of his son Salim (Jahangir). It was abandoned within about 15 years, mostly because of water-supply problems. Key monuments there — Buland Darwaza, Jama Masjid, Panch Mahal, Tomb of Salim Chishti. UNESCO WHS 1986.

questions.stem: The 'Ain-i-Akbari', a detailed account of the administration of Akbar's empire, was written by:
questions.explanation: Abul Fazl, one of Akbar's 'nine jewels' (Navaratnas), wrote the three-volume 'Akbarnama', the third volume of which is the 'Ain-i-Akbari'. He was assassinated in 1602 by Raja Bir Singh Bundela on the orders of Prince Salim (Jahangir). Badauni wrote the more critical 'Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh'. Ferishta wrote 'Tarikh-i-Ferishta' on the Deccan sultanates; Nizamuddin Ahmad wrote 'Tabaqat-i-Akbari'.

questions.stem: Aurangzeb reimposed which tax on non-Muslims in 1679, reversing Akbar's earlier abolition of it?
questions.explanation: Jizya — a poll-tax on non-Muslims — was abolished by Akbar in 1564 and by his grandson Jahangir. Aurangzeb reimposed it in 1679; the move deepened Rajput and Sikh disaffection. Zakat is an obligatory charity on Muslims themselves. Kharaj was the land tax on agricultural produce. Khums was a one-fifth tax on spoils of war.

questions.stem: The famous Peacock Throne, later carried away by Nadir Shah of Persia in 1739, was commissioned by which Mughal emperor?
questions.explanation: Shah Jahan commissioned the Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus) around 1635. It was inlaid with emeralds, rubies, diamonds and pearls including the Koh-i-Noor. In 1739, the Persian conqueror Nadir Shah sacked Delhi and carried the throne (and the Koh-i-Noor) to Iran. The throne itself was later broken up after Nadir Shah's death in 1747. Bahadur Shah II (Zafar) was the last Mughal emperor, 1857.
